scenario_user_message: Are mainstream large models basically all decoder-only now? Why has this trend formed?

finalMessages.content: Are mainstream large models basically all decoder-only now? Why has this trend formed?

content.text:
Yeah, that's basically right — the dominant LLMs today (GPT, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemini, Claude, etc.) are decoder-only. It wasn't always obvious this would win; back around 2019-2020 encoder-decoder (T5, BART) and encoder-only (BERT) were all serious contenders. Let me give you the "why."

A few forces pushed things this way:

**One objective, all the data.** Decoder-only models train on next-token prediction over raw text — every token is a training signal, and you don't need paired or labeled data. Encoder-decoder setups often lean on a more structured objective (span corruption, seq2seq pairs). The simplicity of "just predict the next token on the whole internet" scaled beautifully.

**It's a universal interface.** Once you frame everything as text-in, text-out continuation, a single decoder-only model can do translation, summarization, Q&A, coding — all as prompting. You don't need a separate encoder branch. This is the in-context learning story that GPT-3 made famous.

**Simpler and more efficient to scale.** One stack instead of two. And a big practical win: during generation you can cache past keys/values (KV cache), so autoregressive decoding is efficient. Encoder-decoder cross-attention adds machinery that's harder to scale cleanly.

**Empirically it just held up.** There's real research comparing architectures at scale under matched compute, and decoder-only with a plain language-modeling objective turned out to be a very strong baseline — especially for zero-shot generalization after pure LM pretraining.

One nuance worth flagging so you don't over-generalize: encoder-only models (BERT-style) are still very much alive for embedding and retrieval tasks, where you want a rich bidirectional representation of a fixed input rather than generation. And encoder-decoder still shows up in things like translation and some multimodal setups. "Decoder-only won" is true for *generative chat/LLM* use, not literally everything.

Does the reasoning make sense so far, or do you want me to dig into any one of these — say, why bidirectional encoding actually helps for embeddings but hurts for generation?

stop_reason: end_turn

summary_result.topic: Why decoder-only architectures have become dominant for mainstream LLMs, versus encoder-only and encoder-decoder designs.
key_takeaways: Mainstream generative LLMs (GPT, Llama, Mistral, Qwen, Gemini, Claude) are now overwhelmingly decoder-only, though around 2019-2020 encoder-only (BERT) and encoder-decoder (T5, BART) were serious contenders.
Decoder-only won largely because next-token prediction is a single simple objective that uses every token as a training signal on raw unlabeled text, which scaled well across the whole internet.
Framing all tasks as text-in/text-out continuation gives a universal prompting interface (in-context learning, popularized by GPT-3), avoiding the need for a separate encoder branch.

A single stack is simpler and cheaper to scale, and autoregressive decoding benefits from KV caching, whereas encoder-decoder cross-attention adds machinery that is harder to scale; matched-compute research also showed decoder-only LM pretraining is a strong zero-shot baseline.

Decoder-only 'winning' applies to generative chat/LLM use, not everything — encoder-only models remain preferred for embeddings/retrieval (bidirectional representations) and encoder-decoder still appears in translation and some multimodal setups.
